one_liner: Kernel-bypass C++ datacenter RPC library over DPDK UDP or InfiniBand, near FaSST/RDMA speed on lossy Ethernet.
what_it_does: eRPC is an asynchronous request/response RPC library for machines on the same datacenter network. It runs over lossy Ethernet (UDP through DPDK) or InfiniBand/RoCE and handles packet loss, congestion, node failure, nested RPCs, and messages up to 8 MB. The API is its own and callback-based. You create one Nexus per process, register handlers by request type, create one Rpc endpoint per thread, open sessions with create_session(), then send with enqueue_request(session, type, &req, &resp, continuation, tag) and poll run_event_loop(). Requests and responses must live in hugepage MsgBuffers from the Rpc's allocator. It has no sockets, HTTP, or TLS layer.
how_it_is_fast: Each user thread polls its own NIC queue from userspace and runs short handlers to completion inside the event loop. Longer handlers can go to up to 8 eRPC background threads. The paper's common-case optimizations are zero-copy, single-DMA msgbufs (packet 1's header sits before the data and later headers go at the end), request handlers that read directly from the RX ring, preallocated MTU-sized responses, multi-packet RQ, and unsignaled, batched TX. The wire protocol is client-driven: a session's packet credits are capped near one bandwidth-delay product, and eRPC relies on large dynamic switch buffers so that loss stays rare. Congestion control is Timely plus a Carousel-style timing-wheel rate limiter. When a session is uncongested it skips the Timely update and the wheel and reads rdtsc once per batch, which cuts congestion-control overhead from 20% to 9%. The transports are picked at compile time through a template parameter (static polymorphism), so there are no virtual calls.
when_to_use: Service-to-service or storage RPC where you own both ends and run on bare-metal Mellanox CX3–CX5 or other DPDK-capable 10 GbE+ NICs, and you want a few microseconds of median latency (paper: 2.3 µs on 40 GbE CX5, 3.7 µs on 25 GbE CX4)
Small, fixed-size requests (32 B class) at high rate: in the paper one core handles ~10M RPCs/s when it is both client and server in an all-to-all cluster of about 10 or more nodes
Replication or key-value work that would otherwise need RDMA or PFC: the paper runs a stock Raft port at 5.5 µs 3-way replication and Masstree at 2.7 µs median GET on lossy Ethernet
Bulk transfers up to 8 MB per message on a fast link: up to 75 Gbps on one core over 100 Gbps InfiniBand (raise the 1024 B DPDK MTU constant for bandwidth on Ethernet)
Research baselines where you need a general RPC layer within ~18% of FaSST's small-RPC rate and within 800 ns of RDMA-read latency
when_not_to_use: Anything that must speak HTTP or TLS, or talk to clients that are not eRPC: the UDP/IB wire protocol is custom, so it does not replace any of the HTTP servers in this category

Public-cloud VMs, containers, dev laptops, or setups without root: it needs hugepages (at least 1024 per NUMA node), DPDK owning the NIC port or ibverbs, and NIC flow steering. Only Azure accelerated networking is documented, and the author notes that cloud guests often lack flow steering (issue #44)
Low-rate or bursty callers that sleep between RPCs: latency grows with idle time (issues #104/#116), and the fix PR #123 is still unmerged
Non-x86 hosts: timing uses the rdtsc instruction via inline asm and the build uses -march=native. An aarch64 port needs patches and trips the TSC-frequency assert (issue #111, open)

Long-lived production dependencies: the last commit was 2024-05-09 and the authors now point new users to microsoft/machnet. Networks with more than ~0.01% loss or with packet reordering also hurt it: reordered packets are dropped and handled with go-back-N and a 5 ms RTO, and 8 MB throughput falls to 18 Gbps at 1e-4 loss

integration.dependencies: DPDK 21.11 (dpdk transport; README says other versions are unsupported) or rdma-core/ibverbs (infiniband/RoCE transport); libnuma, pthread, rt; bundled gflags, HdrHistogram_c, googletest and asio headers; 2 MB hugepages; optional libpmem for some apps
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake with pkg-config for DPDK; author reports GCC 7.4 works (issue #33); builds with -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic, so newer compilers may fail (issue #65 open)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 only in practice (rdtsc inline asm, -march=native); NICs: Mellanox CX3–CX5 tested, any DPDK NIC with flow steering, Azure DPDK VMs; a WIN32 DPDK path exists in CMakeLists but is not documented; aarch64 unsupported
integration.thread_safety: One Rpc endpoint per user thread. rpc.h says none of the Rpc functions are thread-safe for user threads, and session and event-loop calls must come from the creating thread. Only eRPC's own background threads may call alloc/enqueue_request/enqueue_response. There is one Nexus per process (multiple Nexus in one process is open issue #84).

gotchas: Idle gaps inflate latency. TimingWheel::reap() advances one slot at a time with no fast-forward, and enqueue_request stamps a stale event-loop TSC, so a request after more than 5 ms idle is falsely retransmitted. The workaround is to keep calling run_event_loop_once() instead of sleeping. The fix is PR #123, open since 2026-08-06.

Most tuning is compile-time. kSessionReqWindow = 8 outstanding requests per session, kSessionCredits = 32, kNumRxRingEntries = 4096 (so about 128 sessions per Rpc before create_session returns -ENOMEM), kRpcRTOUs = 5000, and kMTU = 1024 B on DPDK. Two-machine tests do not reach the 10M RPC/s figure (issue #35: ~1.5 Mrps; issue #121: 3.1 vs 5 Mrps on 10 xl170 nodes).

Buffer ownership is strict. With kZeroCopyRX, a single-packet request buffer is valid only during the handler. A response must use the ReqHandle's pre_resp_msgbuf_ or dyn_resp_msgbuf_, not your own buffer, and eRPC owns request and response msgbufs until the continuation runs. Message size is capped at 8 MB.

Session setup goes over kernel UDP on the management network (ports 31850+n, reachable by hostname), not over the DPDK port. By default only one process can use a DPDK port; the multi-process daemon has been seen stuck in rte_eth_tx_burst (#118). The Nexus segfaults when CPUs are offline, for example with HT disabled (#31; the fix PR #36 has been open since 2019).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick eRPC over Demikernel, Shenango, or FlexTOE when both ends are your own C++ code and you want finished RPC semantics (at-most-once execution, loss recovery, congestion control, nested and background handlers) at millions of small RPCs per core. Pick those siblings when you need a TCP or sockets-style path that other software can talk to, such as Demikernel's DPDK TCP stack or Shenango serving memcached. The HTTP servers here (Drogon, H2O, Lwan, Crow) solve a different problem and are not alternatives.
verified_claims_summary: In the NSDI'19 paper, one thread per node on 11 CloudLab CX4 nodes (25 GbE ConnectX-4 Lx, Xeon E5-2640 v4), with 32 B RPCs, batch size 3 and congestion control on, issued 4.96 Mrps and served as many, so about 10M RPCs/s per core. That is up to 18% below FaSST's numbers from the same CX3 InfiniBand cluster. Median latency was 2.3 µs against 2.0 µs for RDMA reads on CX5. The larger wins are comparisons across papers on different hardware, never re-measured: about 6.7x IX's published 1.5M 64 B RPCs/s, Raft at 5.5 µs against NetChain's published 9.7 µs, and roughly 10x lower GET latency than Cell. The paper names no compiler; the repo builds RelWithDebInfo with -march=native and -flto.
status_note: Stale since the last commit on 2024-05-09 (last release v0.2, 2021), with 19 open issues and 5 open PRs, including the unmerged idle-latency fix. The authors point new users to microsoft/machnet. It is Apache-2.0 (per LICENSE and README; GitHub shows NOASSERTION) and about 6,200 lines of C++ per the paper, so it can be vendored, but expect to own DPDK and rdma-core version pinning yourself.
